claims.text: Room-temperature high-pressure torsion at approximately 6 GPa for 10 rotations will produce an ultrafine-grained microstructure in a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The HPT-produced grains will be sub-micron in size.
Grain refinement will increase the density and area of grain boundaries.
The increased grain-boundary density will provide a higher density of radiation-defect sinks.
The increased grain-boundary area will promote absorption and recombination of irradiation-induced point defects.
Enhanced point-defect absorption and recombination will reduce defect-cluster formation.
Enhanced point-defect absorption and recombination will reduce void growth and irradiation-induced swelling.
The refined grain structure will increase strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
HPT processing will significantly reduce irradiation-induced defect accumulation relative to a conventionally processed coarse-grained alloy.
The reduction in irradiation-induced defect accumulation and swelling could be as large as approximately 40%.
HPT-processed samples will maintain or improve tensile properties relative to conventionally processed samples.
The predicted radiation-tolerance and tensile-property benefits depend on retention of the ultrafine-grained structure during thermal cycling.

A conventionally processed coarse-grained tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy exhibits greater irradiation-induced defect accumulation than the proposed HPT-processed alloy under similar irradiation conditions.

A conventionally processed coarse-grained tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy exhibits lower mechanical performance than the proposed HPT-processed alloy under similar irradiation conditions.
Prolonged high-temperature irradiation or thermal cycling could cause grain growth in the HPT-processed alloy.
Prolonged high-temperature irradiation or thermal cycling could cause embrittlement in the HPT-processed alloy.
